title: DeltaTTG: Training Multi-Turn Agents with a Token-to-Go Progress Meter
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) for multi-turn agents relies on sparse terminal rewards that say little about individual steps. Within-group step comparisons depend on reliable state matching and sufficiently diverse sampled outcomes, while direct step scoring may require costly external evaluators, human annotations, or task-specific heuristics. We introduce DeltaTTG to learn a reusable progress signal through a shared progress meter, using low-cost supervision from diverse policies' recorded trajectories without task-specific progress rules. Its supervision target, Token-to-Go (TTG), the number of tokens remaining to be generated until task completion, serves as an observable proxy for remaining completion effort. During actor training, changes in the frozen meter's estimates redistribute outcome-derived advantages across steps without altering the reward, preserving each trajectory's advantage sign and token-average scale. On ALFWorld, PaperSearchQA, and BFCLv3, DeltaTTG improves the average score over GRPO by 5.7 and 7.2 points with Qwen3-4B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, respectively, outperforms all compared RL baselines on average, and keeps actor-training GPU-hours close to GRPO. Further experiments show improved sample efficiency and out-of-domain performance, and support the meter's ability to distinguish step quality and guide test-time action selection across actor sizes. The code is available at https://github.com/Xuyan923r/DeltaTTG.

title: Deep learning-based virtual perturbation reveals increasing heterogeneity of gene regulatory responses with aging
abstract: A central hypothesis in aging biology proposes that the gradual accumulation of stochastic molecular damage drives transcriptional deregulation (TD), ultimately leading to functional decline. However, existing single-cell analyses largely rely on static expression measurements and provide limited resolution of how regulatory responses change at the level of individual cells. Here, we leverage DKO, a deep learning framework that predicts cell-specific virtual gene perturbation effects from unperturbed transcriptomes, capturing cell-to-cell differences in regulatory context without requiring a reconstructed gene regulatory network or matched perturbation data. Applying DKO to single-cell transcriptomic datasets from humans, mice, Drosophila, and C. elegans revealed that the transcriptional consequences of perturbing the same gene became increasingly heterogeneous across cells with age, indicating that gene regulatory responses become less consistent and more dependent on cellular context. Furthermore, we find that cells with higher somatic mutation burdens have greater knockout-response variability, linking accumulated molecular damage to regulatory inconsistency. Within the same cellular populations, higher impact variability was also associated with higher senescence scores, linking transcriptional dysregulation to senescence-associated states. Our findings identify a progressive loss of regulatory robustness at both the gene and cell levels as a conserved feature of aging, linking stochastic molecular damage to increasing heterogeneity in cellular regulatory responses.

title: Can Agents Truly Forget? Explore Machine Unlearning for LLM Agents
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents have shown strong capabilities in interactive problem solving, tool use, and long-horizon task execution. However, they may also acquire sensitive or private knowledge during training and expose it during deployment. Retraining a model from scratch to remove such knowledge is prohibitively costly, making machine unlearning a more practical approach. Machine unlearning aims to remove targeted undesirable knowledge from trained models without retraining from scratch while preserving general utility. When language models are deployed as agents, parameter-level unlearning becomes insufficient: forgotten information may still persist in memory artifacts or be reacquired via tool calls. In this paper, we formulate the problem of agent unlearning as removing private information from an LLM-based agent across three information channels: parametric knowledge, persistent memory, and tool-call acquisition. To study this problem, we introduce we introduce Agent Unlearning Benchmark (AUBench), a controlled benchmark that extends the fictitious-author setting of TOFU into an agent environment with persistent memory, an offline web snapshot, tool-accessible documents, and provenance-tracked interaction trajectories. By evaluating existing parameter-level and memory-level unlearning methods in this setting, AUBench reveals the gap between model-level forgetting and system-level agent unlearning, and provides a foundation for developing unlearning methods that operate across the full lifecycle of LLM agents.

title: CyberArena: Benchmarking AI Agents in Live Symmetric Attack-and-Defense Combat
abstract: AI agents are demonstrating increasingly strong offensive and defensive cybersecurity capabilities in the real world. Current benchmarks mostly evaluate agents in isolation against static targets. Real cyber operations, however, are dynamic and coupled: security postures constantly change as attackers and defenders adapt to each other in real time. Static benchmarks quickly saturate and miss an agent's ability to attack and defend simultaneously under live pressure. To address this gap, we present CyberArena, a dynamic, symmetric adversarial benchmark built around multi-round attack-and-defense combat. In isolated sandboxes, two agents compete under identical rules, acting concurrently as both attackers and defenders over continuously changing services. This converts static targets into evolving, semi-open challenges, directly testing an agent's speed and precision in discovering, exploiting, and patching vulnerabilities. To sustain the benchmark's longevity, an automated agentic pipeline continuously generates, reviews, and validates new environments. Furthermore, because pairwise contests are notoriously hard to quantify, we introduce a dynamical model that maps match dynamics into unified, multidimensional scores across offensive, defensive, and domain-specific capabilities. Evaluating 12 frontier LLM agents across 40 challenges in 466 matches, CyberArena separates model capabilities where single-agent baselines hit a ceiling. The trajectories read like a fight rather than an exam: defenders patch one hole and miss the next and certify repairs on stale evidence, while capable agents think a move ahead, planting backdoors for later rounds and, in one case, writing their own packet sniffer to watch the opponent. Beyond a benchmark, CyberArena serves as an adaptable, scalable experimental platform for future research on cybersecurity agents.

title: Open-o3-Video-v2: Seek, Ground, and Reason with Verifiable Spatio-Temporal Evidence
abstract: Reliable video reasoning requires models to produce correct answers and expose supporting visual evidence. Open-o3-Video enables verifiable reasoning by embedding timestamps and object-level bounding boxes into reasoning traces, but is restricted to frames from an initial sparse sampler. We introduce Open-o3-Video-v2, which formulates video reasoning as a unified agentic evidencegrounded process. The model identifies missing information, acquires additional observations, grounds the moments and objects supporting its reasoning, and writes this evidence into the trajectory before continuing or answering. To support this behavior, we construct STGR-v2-CoT135K, including 52K multi-turn agentic grounded reasoning trajectories, and STGR-v2-RL-13K for reinforcement learning. We further propose Clue-Seek GRPO (CS-GRPO), which tracks how tool calls change accumulated evidence, rewards clue coverage and step-wise gains, and penalizes excessive, repetitive, or uninformative retrieval. On V-STaR, Open-o3-Video-v2-4B achieves 40.4% mAM and 56.3% mLGM, outperforming its Qwen3-VL-4B backbone by 8.5% and 12.6%, respectively. It also delivers consistent gains across general video understanding, long-video reasoning, and temporal grounding benchmarks. These results show that active evidence acquisition and verifiable object-level grounding are complementary for reliable video reasoning. The code and models are released at https://msalab-pku.github.io/projects/Open-o3-Video-v2.

title: Pack Light, CarryOn: Building Object-Oriented Context for Long-Horizon Agents
abstract: Long-horizon agents accumulate progress in persistent task state, yet repeatedly process interaction histories describing how that progress was achieved. This raises a natural question: can long-horizon context instead be organized around reusable progress rather than the history that produced it? In this paper, we introduce CarryOn, an object-oriented context runtime that organizes continuation around reusable task objects. Rather than treating compressed histories or reconstructed accounts of progress as the primary basis for continuation, CarryOn builds a context view from continuation carriers, complementary execution context, and a live tail of recent interactions. A core challenge is keeping this reusable basis valid after its surrounding history is retired: how can CarryOn update the basis without reconstructing the full representation at every fold? CarryOn maintains carrier records across folds, revising affected records against bound evidence and applicable environment checks while carrying forward unaffected records and jointly updating execution context. Experiments on OSWorld 2.0 and BrowseComp-Plus show improved gains of 5.8% and 7.0% while reducing total token usage by 51.9% and 22.9%, respectively. Project page: https://ethannju.github.io/carryon

title: Decouple to Forget: Semantic Mediation for Sensitive Unlearning in Large Language Models
abstract: Machine unlearning for large language models seeks to remove specified knowledge while preserving general capability, yet current methods often treat an entire response as the unit of forgetting. This coarse granularity causes unnecessary utility loss when the forget target is only a small set of sensitive facts embedded within otherwise benign explanations. In this paper, we introduce Decouple to Forget (D2F), a targeted unlearning method inspired by semantic mediation that separates sensitive factual content from non-sensitive meaning and surface expression. For each example to be forgotten, D2F extracts a fact-level "mediator" representation from the answer, identifies which parts are sensitive, and removes only those parts while leaving the rest of the structure intact. We then generate counterfactual answers grounded in this mediator that preserve non-sensitive content but exclude sensitive facts, employing preference-based contrastive optimization to reduce the likelihood of information leakage while maintaining helpfulness and fluency. Experiments across various benchmark datasets show that D2F achieves a better balance between forgetting and retention than strong baseline methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/JingyueCong/D2F.

title: Looking Complete Is Not Being Grounded: Evaluating LLM Sitreps Against Human-Authored Situation Reports
abstract: Evaluation for automatic crisis reporting should measure what practitioners need, not what is convenient to compare. Through LLM-assisted, author-approved content analysis, we derive a 15-slot information schema from professional humanitarian situation reports using qualitative content analysis, then evaluate 121 human and 261 LLM-generated reports across five disasters and three hazard types. Under google/gemini-3.7-flash on Cyclone Idai, the best machine arm is nominally above the empirical human ceiling (0.827 vs. 0.821), but the difference is statistically indistinguishable from zero (95\% bootstrap CI [-.049,.059]; permutation p=.852), and the ordering does not replicate under openai/gpt-5.6-luna. On a blind 100-item Idai sample, the author agrees with the Gemini judge at 0.910 accuracy and unweighted Cohen's κ=.799. All four judges clear the plan's raw-agreement criterion of .7; only Gemini reaches .7 on chance-corrected κ. Across the three primary events, machine reports reproduce 5.4-11.0% of same-day official figures. Across those same events, raw exact-number matching links 14.3-19.6% of official figures and 85.4-90.1% of machine figures to the social stream; manual audit confirms 45/50 declared absences, 4/25 official matches, and 24/25 machine matches semantically. The issuing-provenance gap is positive in all 12 observed event-judge cells: report date, organisation, series, and authority were not supplied at professional-report coverage in any cell. On the three primary events, ROUGE-L is uninformative, BERTScore is negatively associated with completeness after multiplicity correction, and a generic LLM judge changes sign.

title: When Should Enterprise Policy Decisions Be Learned, and When Should They Be Reasoned?
abstract: An enterprise agent that answers under a written policy must choose an action before it says anything: answer, ask for a missing fact, ask for confirmation, call one or several tools, escalate, or refuse. Holding one 27B Korean enterprise model fixed, we vary whether the decision is a generated JSON object or a single constrained token, and whether the model may reason first. On 2800 in-distribution items we did not detect an accuracy difference between the two deployed paths (93.46% vs 94.14%), while they differ about tenfold in restart stability (3.00% of actions flip vs 0.29%); they also differ in reasoning, so this is an operational comparison. On a sealed benchmark of 300 items whose labels come from a hidden executable policy, reasoning is worth +17.3 points [+12.3, +23.0] on exact action. With reasoning off, the format difference was 0.0 points [-4.3, +4.0], a failure to detect an advantage for either interface, not equivalence; with reasoning on it is unresolved. Against a token-matched random control, boundary-targeted supervision moves the two covered boundaries by +17.5 and +20.0 points and leaves a held-out boundary unchanged. In a 3-seed training x reasoning factorial, the sealed-rendering interaction is -4.9 [-8.1, -1.7], consistent with partial substitution. All supervision was Korean. On independently rendered English versions, the model is 0.82 points lower [-2.68, +0.93] with reasoning on, the same order as re-rendering in Korean; the reasoning-off gain from targeted supervision is not stable in either language, so we do not claim transfer. The original text stays private as the confirmatory set. An open-model re-rendering made after these results reproduced the reasoning effect and the English verdict; the interaction kept its sign but did not replicate under item-clustered intervals. We release the model and that re-rendering with gold labels.

title: APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation
abstract: Post-training is crucial for improving text-to-image models, yet existing pipelines typically rely on manually curated training data and fixed training distributions. We introduce APT (Agentic Post-Training), a fully automated framework that adaptively post-trains a base model according to its evolving capability profile. APT coordinates three agents to construct evaluation sets from user requirements, diagnose model-specific strengths and failure modes, and generate reinforcement learning data with an adaptive prompt distribution that emphasizes underperforming capabilities. By repeatedly evaluating, diagnosing, and updating the generator, APT lets the current model's behavior shape its next training tasks, forming a feedback loop inspired by recursive self-improvement. For general-purpose settings without user-specified evaluation scenarios, we further develop an evaluation harness that enables broad and diverse evaluation set generation. Experiments across multiple base models, benchmarks, and generation architectures demonstrate that APT is model-agnostic, benchmark-agnostic, architecture-agnostic, and fully automated.

By repeatedly evaluating, diagnosing, and updating the generator, APT lets the current model's behavior shape its next training tasks, forming a feedback loop inspired by recursive self-improvement. For general-purpose settings without user-specified evaluation scenarios, we further develop an evaluation harness that enables broad and diverse evaluation set generation. Experiments across multiple base models, benchmarks, and generation architectures demonstrate that APT is model-agnostic, benchmark-agnostic, architecture-agnostic, and fully automated.

title: FrameLite: Decision-Oriented Aesthetic Cropping with a Compact Vision-Language Model
abstract: Aesthetic image cropping improves composition by balancing subjects, context, and image boundaries. Large vision-language models bring semantic knowledge to this task, but their scale limits lightweight photography assistance. We propose FrameLite, a compact cropping model built on Qwen3.5-0.8B. Our approach is motivated by the observation that a small model can generate better crops than its first answer suggests. We develop three-stage training to turn this potential into stronger direct predictions. Spatial and composition training establishes localization and framing preferences. Quality-Guided Online Supervision (QOS) then learns the highest-quality complete answers among the current policy's generated candidates. Greedy-Referenced Optimization (GRO) further refines the policy using positive and negative quality differences relative to its current greedy answer. Both online stages use annotation-derived feedback, while inference returns one coordinate answer without search or an external scorer. Experiments show that FrameLite outperforms the compared large-VLM croppers across public benchmarks with a substantially smaller backbone. Controlled studies confirm that selecting high-quality training answers improves the final model beyond online sampling alone. We will release our code and model weights at https://github.com/JianzeLi-114/FrameLite .

title: LensErase: A Foundation Model for Erase Anything
abstract: We introduce LensErase, a general-purpose mask-based Erase Anything foundation model designed to cover a broad spectrum of real-world erase scenarios. LensErase supports diverse objects, visual text, watermarks, associated visual effects, multiple-object removal, and a wide range of object scales, aspect ratios, and image resolutions. First, to enable such broad coverage, we construct LensErase-100M, a large-scale dataset containing 101.07 million paired source-mask-target examples spanning diverse erase scenarios. Second, we pretrain LensErase from the text-to-image model Lens, adapting its strong generative prior to mask-based erasing. To efficiently incorporate the source image and erase mask, we propose Mask-Aware RoPE, a 3D rotary positional encoding that directly injects mask information into the source-image tokens without introducing a separate mask token sequence. Finally, we refine the model through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning with contract-guided, region-aware rewards, and apply TraceFusion at inference to preserve high-fidelity content outside the effective edit region. Across six public benchmarks and the proposed LensErase-Bench, LensErase achieves substantial improvements under both reference-based objective metrics and reference-free VLM evaluation. We hope LensErase can serve as a foundational model for erase-related applications and systems.

title: Acting Through Registers
abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) use generative visual representations to condition robot actions, yet how these representations organize action-relevant information remains poorly understood. We identify persistent high-norm spatial outliers in WAM representations and find that their action relevance persists even after normalization and K/V projection attenuate their extreme magnitude. Motivated by this observation, we introduce RegisterWAM, which adds learnable non-spatial registers to the world model and uses them directly for action conditioning. Registers alone do not fully eliminate spatial outliers; pairing them with observation flow-matching (FM) loss supervision suppresses spatial outliers while concentrating high-norm responses in registers. Beyond this reorganization, observation FM loss supervision also improves action learning without registers, motivating an additional noised-observation FM objective that learns current-scene recovery from corrupted inputs. The resulting model achieves 81.64\% success on LIBERO-Plus without additional embodied pretraining data or foundation models, reaches 93.0\% average success on RoboTwin 2.0, and improves real-world manipulation performance.

title: Training LLMs for Multi-Agent Collaboration with Verifiable Information Rewards
abstract: Effective collaboration among large language model (LLM) agents in multi-agent systems requires sharing relevant evidence, requesting missing information, and incorporating teammates' contributions into decisions. Training these behaviors is challenging because final task outcomes provide limited feedback on the value of individual messages. We introduce CoSIR (Collaboration via Surprisal-based Information Rewards), a post-training approach that uses a simple, verifiable environment to teach collaboration behaviors that generalize to more complex, unseen tasks. We propose a Bayesian evaluator that scores shared information by its reduction in team surprisal, defined as the sum of the negative log probabilities assigned to the correct option given each agent's available evidence. Requests are scored by the potential reduction in the same quantity if the requested information were truthfully provided. Separate rewards encourage agents to use the received information in their private choices and calculations. We post-train Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and Gemma-3-4B-it through self-play and evaluate transfer to seven unseen natural-language collaboration tasks. CoSIR achieves the highest aggregate score, while its performance in general tasks remains competitive. Behavioral analyses show increased disclosure of private evidence and fewer judged failures to use teammates' input.

title: 4LC: 4D Latent Cache for Efficient Conditioning in Dynamic World Modeling
abstract: For video generation in dynamic world modeling, observed static and dynamic content should be efficiently reused to provide conditions for repeated generation at different times and viewpoints. We introduce 4LC, a 4D latent cache with composite visual representations and a flexible spatiotemporal access interface. As a latent cache, 4LC directly reuses visual representations of static and dynamic content to provide generation conditions, avoiding per-request RGB rendering and re-encoding. As a composite cache, 4LC binds visual representations from multiple visual encoders (e.g., VAE, DINO, V-JEPA, VGGT) to shared geometry and motion, allowing the composite representations to describe the dynamic world with rich information. Besides, we design a flexible spatiotemporal interface, which directly reads the cache at independently specified times and viewpoints and combines readouts across observations, providing a common conditioning format for diverse downstream tasks. Building on 4LC, we develop 4LC-Video to address multiple video generation tasks through different configurations of source observations, spatiotemporal requests, and historical reuse, including camera control, temporal control, novel-view synthesis, scene revisits, and long-term generation. Our experiments show more efficient condition acquisition, effective spatiotemporal controllability, and scene consistency across tasks using a single 4LC-Video model without task-specific fine-tuning.

title: RT-J: Large-Scale Pretraining of Relational Transformers for Context-Efficient Predictions
abstract: Foundation models for tables and relational databases are increasingly used for predictive tasks across various scientific and industrial domains. However, adapting existing models to unseen datasets requires tens of thousands of examples. Here we introduce RT-J, an 85M-parameter relational foundation model (RFM) that makes accurate predictions even with hundreds of in-context examples or fewer. To achieve this, we first assemble the Join, a large collection of 639 web-crawled databases with 6,023 LLM-generated forecasting tasks. We pretrain with long contexts of up to 8,192 database cells, using in-context examples from a novel lightweight random-walk retriever. Finally, we leverage context tuning and ensembling to scale up test-time compute. On in-context regression tasks from RelBench, RT-J requires 10x fewer examples on average to match strong feature engineering pipelines with LLM-agent or RDBLearn featurizers and TabICLv2 or LightGBM predictors. Overall, our work pushes the frontier for context-efficient predictions on relational data and highlights the importance of real-world semantics, context engineering and large-scale pretraining for RFMs.

title: Chasing Label Shifters: A Change-Aware Framework for Dynamic Graph Node Classification
abstract: Entities in real-world systems often evolve over time: users shift between information consumption patterns, researchers migrate between fields, and firms transition between financial risk states. When such systems are modeled as dynamic graphs, these transitions correspond to nodes whose class labels change between consecutive snapshots, which we call shifters. Correctly classifying shifters is often more consequential than classifying stable nodes with persistent labels, as detecting such transitions enables timely intervention in high-stakes settings. Yet, we identify a systematic failure mode across all major dynamic graph neural network architectures: shifter performance consistently lags behind stable nodes, with errors concentrated on the old label. Our structural analysis traces this failure to embedding inertia: neighborhood aggregation keeps shifter representations anchored to the old-class centroid, and this effect is strongest precisely where it is hardest to correct, namely for shifters whose neighborhoods remain aligned with the old class. Guided by this finding, we propose CHASE, a model-agnostic CHange-Aware framework for Shifting nodEs that wraps any dynamic GNN with targeted components for detecting label shifts and overriding stale neighborhood signals. CHASE consistently improves shifter performance across all tested models and datasets (up to 114.9% and 202.5% improvement on accuracy and F1 score, respectively) while preserving stable-node performance. We additionally contribute three dynamic graph benchmarks with naturally shifting labels, filling a gap in existing resources. The source code is available at https://github.com/jhkim611/CHASE

title: Smartphone-Based, Field-Deployed AI Inspection System for Power Distribution Infrastructure
abstract: Routine inspection of power distribution infrastructure remains challenging for utilities operating geographically dispersed networks, where conventional manual inspection can be difficult to perform consistently and at scale. This work presents a smartphone-based AI inspection system for assessing targeted distribution-infrastructure conditions from images captured by field personnel. The proposed workflow integrates image-quality and viewing-perspective validation with AI-assisted assessment of pole lean, crossarm and top-cleat tilt, voltage level, vegetation-clearance risk, and distribution-transformer (DTR)-ground clearance. The system integrates deep-learning models with monocular depth estimation, geometric analysis, and rule-based processing within a common multi-stage inspection workflow designed for practical field operation. The system was pilot deployed across five selected distribution feeders within the Eastern Power Distribution Company of Andhra Pradesh Ltd. (APEPDCL), where 1,222 defect instances were identified across the assessed categories and subsequently tracked through a rectification and verification workflow, with 84 defect instances recorded as rectified during the study period. Feeder-level interruption records were also examined over the study period; however, the available observations do not provide sufficient evidence to establish a reliability improvement attributable to the proposed system. A curated multi-module field-captured dataset, PD-Defect, is also publicly released to support reproducible research in distribution-infrastructure inspection. The field deployment demonstrates the practical integration of smartphone-based AI-assisted inspection into field inspection and maintenance activities, providing a mechanism for systematic identification, documentation, rectification tracking, and verification of targeted distribution-infrastructure defects.

title: EdgeWise: Bringing Long-Horizon Agents to the Edge via Selective Cloud Delegation
abstract: Complex and long-horizon agent tasks often rely on frontier models deployed in the cloud to achieve strong performance. However, using these models for every step of a long-horizon trajectory incurs substantial inference cost, even though not all steps may require the same level of model capability. In this paper, we find that allocating the LLM to only a small subset of key steps can achieve performance comparable to full LLM execution while significantly reducing inference cost. Motivated by this observation, we propose EdgeWise, an edge-cloud collaboration framework that deploys an SLM on the local device as the primary solver and selectively delegates critical steps to a cloud LLM when stronger model capacity is needed. To enable autonomous delegation without additional models at inference time, we introduce a step-level RL method that jointly optimizes task solving and delegation, with fine-grained credit assignment for individual delegation decisions. We also introduce an external judge-based delegation strategy and use it to systematically investigate key design choices in edge-cloud collaboration, including when to delegate, how delegation decisions should be made, what context should be shared, and how frequently the cloud LLM should be invoked. Experiments show that EdgeWise matches or outperforms pure-LLM execution while reducing inference cost up to 62% on SWE-Rebench and 34% on Terminal-Bench 2.1. We further deploy EdgeWise on a local workstation, demonstrating comparable cost savings in a practical edge-cloud setting.

title: Copy-Paste Language Models
abstract: Transformers are intuitively considered to be efficient at copying from their inputs. We actually show that the ability of LLMs to copy in context can be improved through explicit modeling. We propose Copy-Paste Language Models (CPLMs), which add a lightweight Copy-Paste head to the conventional language modeling (LM) head. CPLMs improve training efficiency, downstream performance, and offer new operating points in long-context and retrieval setups. We validate our approach by pretraining models from 135M to 1.7B parameters, showing improvements across all scales and backbones with negligible training and inference overheads. We explain the success of CPLMs by showing that they partially mitigate the LM head gradient bottleneck through an alternative gradient path.

title: FlashVSR+: Efficient Video Super-Resolution via Hybrid Attention and Reward-Yield Distribution Matching
abstract: Recent video super-resolution (VSR) models achieve efficient one-step generation through diffusion distillation. However, high-resolution inference remains costly, and distilled models are difficult to align with human preferences. These challenges call for improvements in both model architecture and training strategy. We present FlashVSR+ to address both limitations. On the architecture side, we introduce hybrid attention based on the strong locality observed in pretrained VSR models, while retaining sparse global interaction for long-range consistency. It achieves up to 2times DiT speedup and 45\% lower peak memory, enabling spatially untiled 4K VSR on a single 24GB RTX 4090. On the training side, we propose Reward-Yield Distribution Matching Distillation (Ry-DMD) for preference-aligned one-step generation. Ry-DMD uses reward-weighted teacher rollouts to incorporate black-box rewards into distribution matching, without backpropagating through the reward model. We further show that Ry-DMD generalizes beyond VSR to T2I generation. Together, FlashVSR+ delivers stronger restoration quality and substantially improves high-resolution efficiency, with consistent gains in user preference. We release our code, models, and training data at https://www.flashvsr.tech{FlashBlue{www.flashvsr.tech}}.

title: Into the LidarVerse: A Real-Time Unified LiDAR World Model Across Tasks and Sensors
abstract: We present LidarVerse, a real-time unified LiDAR world model for sensor simulation across tasks and sensors. Existing LiDAR simulators largely follow one of two complementary paradigms: reconstruction-based methods preserve the geometry of a captured scene but require lengthy per-scene optimization, whereas generative methods amortize learning across data but lack the consistency needed for long-horizon rollouts. LidarVerse brings both paradigms into a single, unified conditional generative framework. A universal tokenizer maps LiDAR range sequences into a shared latent space, where a bidirectional teacher learns a common interface for conditioning on a LiDAR prefix, an HD-Map, a persistent spatial cache, and optionally, text. Varying the available scene evidence turns the same model into a generator of new worlds, a point-cloud forecaster, or a generalizable resimulator of observed scenes without per-scene optimization. We distill the teacher into a four-step autoregressive causal student and maintain both a rolling temporal K/V cache and a world-aligned spatial cache, enabling persistent long-horizon rollouts with real-time inference at 11 FPS on a single H100 GPU. LidarVerse achieves state-of-the-art performance on most reported metrics across all three evaluation protocols, while its tokenizer supports 32-, 64-, and 128-beam LiDAR and generalizes to an unseen scanning pattern. These results demonstrate that generative and reconstruction-grounded LiDAR simulation can be realized within one model, providing the core capabilities for future closed-loop sensor simulation.

title: TacitVLA: Reasoning Vision-Language-Action Models Without Reasoning Latency
abstract: Textual reasoning before acting has improved vision-language-action (VLA) models, but at the cost of latency: every action conditioned on the reasoning text must wait for autoregressive decoding. We show that actions do not need to wait for or condition on the generated reasoning to benefit from it, because the reasoning supervision already improves the backbone representation. We introduce TacitVLA, a reasoning VLA whose action expert never attends to the reasoning it generates for the current call. On long-horizon tasks where the reasoning text also serves as episodic memory, it can generate each entry during action execution rather than before acting. We evaluate it in a controlled study on four benchmarks spanning manipulation and autonomous driving, memory and non-memory tasks: RoboMME, RMBench, LIBERO, and PhysicalAI-AV. On all four, TacitVLA matches the performance of its explicit-reasoning counterpart at up to 3.4x lower latency, and matches the latency of the same architecture trained without reasoning at up to +17.1% success. In absolute terms, it surpasses the best previously published results on the RoboMME Counting suite (82.7% vs. 66.8%) and RMBench (77.5% vs. 56.5%), and reaches 72.9% on LIBERO-Plus and a 52.5% scene score on the public split of the PhysicalAI-AV closed-loop driving challenge. Project page: https://tacitvla.github.io.

On all four, TacitVLA matches the performance of its explicit-reasoning counterpart at up to 3.4x lower latency, and matches the latency of the same architecture trained without reasoning at up to +17.1% success. In absolute terms, it surpasses the best previously published results on the RoboMME Counting suite (82.7% vs. 66.8%) and RMBench (77.5% vs. 56.5%), and reaches 72.9% on LIBERO-Plus and a 52.5% scene score on the public split of the PhysicalAI-AV closed-loop driving challenge. Project page: https://tacitvla.github.io.

title: ListQA: A Benchmark for Evaluating List-Formatted Factual Knowledge Retrieval in Large Language Models
abstract: Many real-world questions demand not a single fact but an organized collection of them, yet existing factual knowledge benchmarks almost exclusively target single answer retrieval. We introduce ListQA, a benchmark of 9,045 human-curated, cross-validated questions (audited error rate of 1.7%) that require LLMs to recall multiple facts and compose them into structured lists of 3-10 elements. Questions range from flat lists ("Which NCAA teams went undefeated between 2000 and 2024?") to hierarchical lists with sub-attributes ("...and what was their record and result?"), spanning eight categories across 60+ countries. An evergreen design (explicit temporal constraints or historically immutable facts) keeps ground truth valid without periodic updates. For evaluation, we frame element matching as a linear sum assignment problem: optimal bipartite matching paired with LLM-based semantic grading jointly captures factual accuracy, hallucination, and format compliance. We benchmark 34 models (8 families, 42 configurations across standard and thinking enabled inference) and find: the best standard-inference model scores below 37% LLM-Judge-F1, multi-faceted questions are harder across the board, and providing the source Wikipedia page lifts scores dramatically, confirming that models can organize facts but struggle to retrieve them from parameters alone. Extended analyses cover base vs. instruction-tuned checkpoints and token efficiency. We release the dataset and evaluation code.

title: Designing Protein Structures from Natural Language
abstract: A central challenge in de novo protein design is generating proteins with desired structural and functional properties. Existing design models typically require a dedicated input representation for each property, limiting the design objectives they support. We develop Prompteina, the first all-atom structure generation model that supports new and broader design objectives specified in natural language, analogous to text-to-image generation. To train Prompteina, we construct Prompteina-Data, a paired text--protein structure dataset of 1.8M structures and 50M+ captions describing global and residue-specific structural and functional properties. We adapt Proteina-Complexa, a pretrained structure generation model, through text-conditioned pretraining and finetuning that aligns residues with their corresponding text. Prompteina outperforms baselines on 15 of 18 structural properties and generates proteins that more closely match descriptions of their intended functions. In binder design, it leads baselines on at least 13 of 20 targets and improves interface confidence by 14% over the strongest baseline. With iterative in silico feedback, Prompteina's gain over non-iterative generation is 57% larger than the next-best baseline on the hardest targets. Finally, we experimentally validate Prompteina designs against GM2A, a target with no reported de novo binders. We identify nine binders, with the strongest at an apparent K_{D} of 107 nM. These results establish natural language as an effective and powerful conditioning interface for protein structure generation.

title: Into the Unknown: Benchmarking AI agents on open scientific research problems
abstract: Can AI agents carry out research on open scientific problems? We introduce Into the Unknown, a benchmark that provides an agent with a science paper along with a research direction to pursue and tasks it to write a follow-up paper. We work with scientists at US Department of Energy (DOE) national laboratories, who each contribute an unpublished follow-up direction from their own work together with the necessary conditions a submission must meet. While assessing the quality of a follow-up paper is challenging in general, using these conditions to form a rubric makes evaluation more tractable for research problems that have no reference answer. We have nine frontier agents write 15 follow-ups each, spanning quantum computing, plasma physics, computational chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning domains. None of the 135 submissions satisfies all the conditions, and 114 fail our integrity check, most often because the paper claims work that was never done or reports numbers that contradict the recorded evidence. Overall, agents readily produce papers that look like follow-ups, but none meets the standard of the domain scientist, leaving substantial headroom. Our code and data are publicly available.

title: UniDeblur: Unified Motion Deblurring via Fourier Convolution Learning
abstract: Image deblurring is a fundamental task in computer vision, yet existing methods mainly specialize in isolated scenarios. Consequently, the deblurring performance of these models drops significantly across scenarios with different cameras and image contents. This motivates the development of a unified motion deblurring framework that can handle diverse blur patterns. To this end, we construct a multi-source dataset and develop a data pruning and quality control pipeline. Then, to restore blur images with various motion blur kernels across different scenarios, we propose a unified motion deblurring framework via Fourier Convolution Learning. Existing deblurring networks usually rely on pixel-level mappings and overlook the convolutional nature of blur. Thus, the network mostly fits the image content itself rather than learning the convolution process, making it difficult to handle multi-source blur images. Instead of relying on spatial mapping, we perform blur-adaptive global filter learning in Fourier space, which avoids the limited spatial support of kernel estimation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our unified model effectively handles motion blurs across diverse sources and scenes, achieving competitive performance across both in-domain and OOD benchmarks. Code has been released at github.com/DeepMed-Lab-ECNU/Single-Image-Deblur.

title: MA-Bench: Measuring Operational Planning in Language Models
abstract: How well can a language model turn a large, incomplete and partly contradictory body of documents into a plan when no single correct answer exists? We introduce Mission Analysis (MA)-Bench, built on mission analysis, the first step of military operational planning, in which a staff reads the full situation and states the problem before anyone proposes a solution. Its 10 expert-built scenarios pair synthetic packets of ten to twelve documents with 1,257 expert-written pass/fail requirements, each containing information on their source, question type, and importance level. A reasoning-model judge grades each brief against the requirements without seeing the documents; it grades like a fifth credentialed planner, leaving a four-planner panel's agreement unchanged (Fleiss κ 0.42 to 0.41), and a judge from a second provider reproduces the model ranking (Spearman 0.94). Across twenty frontier and open-weights models the best gets 62% of the rubric items right. Models are strongest on facts stated in the documents (58%) and weakest on judgments that must be inferred (33%), and six failures in ten are omissions rather than errors. MA-Bench grades the determinations, not the prose. We release the packets, rubrics, prompts, scorer and every graded brief with item-level verdicts.

title: Telling FIBS: Probes Effectively Detect Sabotage and Catch Unverbalized Deception
abstract: Recent incidents have highlighted the challenge of monitoring LLM agents and the danger of models deceiving people. We show that white-box deception detection via probes can be scaled up to frontier monitoring settings by collecting the largest deception dataset to date for training probes and introducing a novel probe architecture which can aggregate information across many layers and tokens. Our probes achieve 98.4\% AUROC in SHADE-Arena and 98.0\% in BASH-Arena (vs. 97.9\%, 97.6\% resp. for action-only text monitors) and show improved efficacy as the underlying model is scaled up. We further test probes on several cases where deception cannot be determined from the context alone. In these cases, which we refer to as introspective deception, the ground truth can only be determined through careful elicitation or thorough knowledge of a model's training data. In one such evaluation, we show that probes can distinguish transcripts containing a model's true hidden goal from other goals with an AUROC of up to 99.7\%. Our probes also readily detect deception on prominent open-weight models which lie about politically sensitive topics, and about their beliefs when put under pressure. We release our training dataset, dubbed \fibs, to help drive frontier deployment of effective probes, and encourage the community to expand upon it with further examples of deception and sabotage.

title: CAFE: Confining Feature Distillation to Language-Routed Adapters for Compact Multilingual Automatic Speech Recognition
abstract: Feature distillation is usually expected to add to logit distillation. We find that this expectation does not hold for two common feature losses in compact multilingual automatic speech recognition (ASR), and analyze why through their gradients. The gradient of a projection-based loss is orthogonal to the task gradient, while that of Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA), a similarity-based loss, is weakly aligned with it. CKA lowers the word error rate (WER) on non-English languages, but at the expense of data-rich English. Three loss-level remedies (one trained, two probed) all fall short, and the CKA gradient overlaps with the subspace English uses in the shared encoder by 97.5% to 99.5% (about 81% by chance). Guided by this diagnosis, we propose CAFE (Confined-Adapter Feature distillation), which confines the CKA gradient to adapters that English bypasses, addressing the trade-off in the parameters rather than in the loss. On the Open ASR Leaderboard, CAFE lowers the average WER from 8.55% to 8.02%, beats an adapter-only capacity control at 8.51%, and makes English more stable across checkpoints. At 254M parameters, it trails the 0.6B teacher by 2 WER points and is competitive with much larger models across 48 test sets in 24 languages. We use 564k hours of training data and state-of-the-art models to keep the findings relevant to practice.

title: Nonlinear Schrödinger equation in an exterior domain
abstract: We study the exact controllability of the cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation in the exterior Ω=R^nsetminusΘ of a non-trapping obstacle Θ, with internal controls supported outside a large ball, and the corresponding boundary control problem on Ω_0=B_{R_0}setminusΘ with Dirichlet controls acting only on the outer sphere partial B_{R_0}. Using the local smoothing effect of Burq, Gérard and Tzvetkov [9], we prove observability inequalities for the linear Schrödinger equation in the whole scale of Sobolev spaces H^σ_D(Ω), σin[-2,2], associated with the Dirichlet Laplacian; they require only the non-trapping assumption (no star-shapedness of Θ), and their proofs use no normal boundary traces. Combined with Strichartz-type estimates and a perturbation argument, this yields local exact controllability in H^1_0(Ω) and in H^2(Ω)cap H^1_0(Ω), in dimensions two and three, around the zero solution and, for internal controls and under a unique continuation assumption, around nontrivial trajectories. The same method applies to the quintic equation, which is energy-critical in dimension three. Several open problems are discussed.

title: CLASHarness: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Conflict in Computer Use via a Controllable and Verifiable Generation Pipeline
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent systems to automate complex computer-use workflows, yet existing benchmarks mostly assume consistent, cooperative environments. In contrast, real-world collaboration rarely runs on consistent information: peer or sub-agents frequently report outdated states, issue contradictory instructions, or compete over shared permissions and files, forcing agents to check others' outputs and verify ground truth in the environment. Evaluating such conflict resolution remains challenging: manual authoring cannot scale across complex systems, while unconstrained LLM generation produces narrative drift, answer leakage, and unsatisfiable rubrics. We introduce CLASHarness (Conflict-Loaded Agent Scenario Harness), a controllable framework for generating verifiable multi-agent conflicts in computer use, with a benchmark of 600 multi-round tasks. By combining hierarchical scenario planning with an eight-step verified micro-pipeline, CLASHarness pre-commits decisive visual facts before rendering and compiles hybrid code and semantic graders directly from executed reference trajectories, guaranteeing every task is solvable by construction. Evaluating 15 frontier models on CLASHarness reveals three core bottlenecks. First, when sub-agent outputs conflict with the environment, weaker models blindly follow misleading information, whereas stronger models inspect visual evidence to verify ground truth. Second, resolving conflicts is much harder than finding them: while agents can spot inconsistencies, actively fixing system state drops task success significantly. Third, coordination protocols remain a universal bottleneck: even frontier models fail over 58% of closing actions, often forgetting to release shared locks or hand off tasks. CLASHarness provides a scalable, verifiable foundation for building reliable multi-agent systems.

title: WARP-VLA: Wrist-Camera Adaptation for View-Robust Policy Execution in Vision-Language-Action Models
abstract: Despite recent advances in Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) for robotic manipulation, their performance remains sensitive to changes in camera configuration. The problem becomes more evident in cross-setup deployment, as reproducing the exact camera pose used for training is nearly impossible. Unlike fixed external views, wrist views are more challenging because the camera moves with the robot, causing even small mounting variations to alter fine-grained geometric cues. To address this, we propose WARP-VLA, a camera-view robust VLA for diverse wrist camera configurations. WARP-VLA adopts a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture where individual experts learn view-specific feature transformations, and a router combines them based on implicit view information. This allows the policy to be deployed without requiring camera extrinsic parameters as additional input. Through experiments on the LIBERO benchmark, WARP-VLA improves the average success rate of pi-0.5 from 39.2% to 78.3% under wrist-view perturbations. The real-robot experiments further show that the feature-level adaptation learned in simulation successfully transfers to diverse deployment settings. To facilitate reproducibility and future research, we release our wrist viewpoint robustness benchmark and a plug-and-play implementation.

title: Unlocking Structured Pruning for Reasoning Language Models via Attention-Preserving MLP Trimming
abstract: Structured pruning reduces LLM inference costs by removing model components to produce smaller dense models. However, existing methods can cause reasoning performance to collapse on long-form reasoning tasks such as AIME. We propose LayerTrim, a training-free structured pruning method that identifies redundant decoder layers and selectively trims their MLP features while preserving attention and decoder depth. LayerTrim is the first training-free structured pruning method designed to preserve long-form reasoning without gradients or recovery training. Across three reasoning language models and five benchmarks, LayerTrim outperforms existing structured pruning methods in most evaluated settings, improving average accuracy by up to 21.4 percentage points over RESP. On Qwen3-14B, LayerTrim achieves 1.24times faster prefill and 19.7\% lower peak GPU memory than the dense model, while better preserving reasoning ability. It also achieves the shortest average generation length among evaluated pruned models, while retaining the highest average accuracy. These results demonstrate that LayerTrim improves reasoning efficiency through both structural compression and reduced token generation.

title: Open-MMUnlearning: Unifying Methods and Evaluation for MLLM Unlearning
abstract: As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) become more capable and widely deployed, concerns about privacy and safety have become increasingly pressing. Machine unlearning offers one approach to addressing these concerns by removing designated information from trained models while preserving unrelated capabilities. However, fragmented implementations and evaluation protocols, incomplete robustness testing, and limited understanding of metric reliability make progress in MLLM unlearning difficult to assess systematically. We introduce Open-MMUnlearning, an open-source, extensible framework that integrates target-model preparation, multimodal data processing, unlearning, and evaluation through shared interfaces and structured configurations. The framework supports five benchmarks spanning privacy, safety, and copyright, eight MLLMs from four model families, and twelve unlearning methods. Its evaluation suite jointly assesses forgetting effectiveness, retained utility, and robustness to model interventions, adversarial inputs, and membership inference attacks. Using a common evaluation protocol, we compare ten representative unlearning methods. In this comparison, GD and MIP-Editor tie for the highest overall score: GD achieves the highest Forget Quality, while MIP-Editor preserves more Model Utility. We further introduce a metric meta-evaluation protocol that tests faithfulness using models with controlled exposure to target knowledge and robustness under quantization and relearning. Among the thirteen evaluated metrics, BLEU achieves the highest aggregate reliability score. KS-Test attains the highest faithfulness AUC but performs less well on robustness. Together, the framework and these findings support reproducible comparison of MLLM unlearning methods and systematic assessment of evaluation reliability.

title: GroundGUI: GUI Grounding by High-Quality Data and Distillation-to-Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Constructing robust GUI agents relies on multimodal visual grounding: the ability to precisely map natural language intents to actionable on-screen components. Despite abundant desktop, web, and mobile benchmarks, high-fidelity resources tailored for diverse environments are surprisingly scarce. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Screen Referring Grounding Dataset (ScreenRef), a comprehensive GUI grounding dataset consisting of GUI screenshots paired with natural language referring expressions and box or point annotations. Spanning desktop, web, and mobile domains, ScreenRef comprises 586K screenshots and over 633K referring expression instances, covering tasks such as text recognition, visual matching, spatial understanding, and refusal scenarios. To boost the model's grounding performance, we propose the Distillation-to-Reinforcement Learning (D2RL) method to address the limited generalization of supervised fine-tuning and the sparse reward problem in reinforcement learning. Utilizing ScreenRef, we train Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct via sequential SFT and D2RL training, yielding GroundGUI-8B. evidence.title: GroundGUI: GUI Grounding by High-Quality Data and Distillation-to-Reinforcement Learning
evidence.abstract: Constructing robust GUI agents relies on multimodal visual grounding: the ability to precisely map natural language intents to actionable on-screen components. Despite abundant desktop, web, and mobile benchmarks, high-fidelity resources tailored for diverse environments are surprisingly scarce. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Screen Referring Grounding Dataset (ScreenRef), a comprehensive GUI grounding dataset consisting of GUI screenshots paired with natural language referring expressions and box or point annotations. title: SceneFactory-3D: Lifting 2D Traffic Scenes into 3D Physical Counterfactuals for Scalable Physically Grounded Safety Evaluation
abstract: Scalable driving simulators typically execute vehicle commands using prescribed behavioral or kinematic rules, overlooking the physics of tire-road interfaces, thereby limiting their ability to capture how adverse road and environmental conditions alter vehicle execution and propagate through traffic. To address this limitation, we present SceneFactory-3D, a GPU-batched, physics-grounded multi-agent driving simulator. Vehicles execute acceleration and steering commands via suspension- and friction-limited forces evaluated at each wheel-contact point. Spatially varying friction, per-world 3D heightfields, gravity, and rigid contact consistently govern wheel motion and chassis collisions. Per-world terrain isolation and GPU batching enable SceneFactory-3D to run matched physical counterfactuals in parallel: traffic scenario setup and vehicle controllers remain fixed while only the road condition changes, enabling the resulting closed-loop effects to be evaluated across parallel worlds. To demonstrate the advantage of the SceneFactory-3D-enabled counterfactual evaluation, we conduct an empirical study on vehicle controllers' sensitivity to road conditions. We study three learned-policy families on 1,024 matched 12-vehicle worlds per condition, and two classical planners on a shared 32-world subset, across 21 friction and grade conditions. When friction drops from 1.0 to 0.18, the share of vehicles that clear the work zone safely falls by 6 to 90 percentage points across learned policies (18-19 for classical planners), and near-collision situations become more frequent for every learned policy. Code: https://github.com/SmallWorldLab/SceneFactory_3D

title: Tracing Knowledge Lineage for Federated Unlearning under Mutual Distillation
abstract: An edge server and nearby devices can train language models of different sizes together by mutual distillation. Federated unlearning (FU) and unlearning for large language models (LLMs) execute a removal request on one model. Under mutual distillation, however, the effect of the removed data has been copied into many students, and their uploads teach it back to the corrected teacher. We propose Holder-level Erasure via Replication-weighted Delta-closure (HERD), which decides which holders must be corrected. HERD records a knowledge lineage graph from the transfers that the server already performs and weights each edge by its transfer type. It computes how many times the residual at each holder will be copied and selects the cheapest set of holders whose correction bounds the cumulative residual after the request. A transfer guard and a rejoin rule cover the holders left uncorrected or offline. We prove that partial correction suffices only when the copy number of the lineage graph is below one, that averaging alone never reaches one, and that the correction set remains valid under link outages. On TOFU, HERD leaves 18% to 52% less cumulative residual than the strongest baseline at 6% to 12% of its correction cost.
